newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Nomura Intl. tries to ride out scandal.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Nomura Intl. tries to ride out scandal.

text.p: Nomura International Plc, London-based unit of scandal-rocked Japanese broker Nomura Securities, is trying to refocus its business on areas not affected by the controversy surrounding its parent.

But Takashi Tsutsui, currently president and replacing Hitoshi Tonomura as chairman on June 1, admitted to Reuters in an interview that Nomura Intl. had not escaped unscathed from the shock waves of the scandal.

"The main areas affected (in Europe) by the scandal include Japanese-related business, orders from Japanese institutional investors, and underwriting for a certain number of overseas sovereign entities."
Nomura Securities is currently at the centre of a scandal involving suspected payoffs to racketeers.

"There are very few Japanese companies who have recently come to us for issuance of bonds, convertible bonds, and warrants in Europe," Tsutsui said, but added he remained optimistic about current business conditions in Europe.

"Compared with Tokyo, effects (from the scandal) on operations in London and across Europe are very small. We think confidence (of customers) in our services and business has not been hurt. When the scandal comes to an end, I believe the customers (who have left) will return," he said.

Revenues for the year ending in March in Nomura's overall European operations including Nomura International rose almost nine pct from a year ago to well over 400 million pounds, while pre-tax current profits increased more than 17 pct to about 80 million pounds, he said.
Nomura made a profit in overall European operations in April, he said, adding, "We are doing okay in May."
"I can't tell what the results will be for the April-September period, but we are optimistic (that there will be profits)," he said.
Asked if he thinks that revenues and profits for the year ending in March 1998 would be more than the previous year, Tsutsui said: "Lots of things could happen. We hope so, but we don't know."
Tsutsui said the areas Nomura would focus on included activities in emerging markets in eastern Europe, securitisation, coporate finance in Europe, and networks in areas such as the U.S. and Asia.
In eastern Europe, Nomura has so far mostly dealt with governments, but has just started to expand its business into the corporate sector, he said.
He expected to expand securitisation, in which Nomura is active mainly in the U.K., into other European nations.
Asked about the recent yen surge which caused losses to some Japanese brokers which underwrote yen-based dual currency bonds, he said Nomura would continue in the market.

"The products themselves are good as they meet investors requirements by offering high interest rates outside Japan when Japnaese interestes are at such low levels. As long as we don't get caught with bad timing, the products are good."
Tsutsui also said Nomura's business was unlikely to be affected by whether the U.K. joined the European economic and monetary union (EMU) or not.

"The most important thing is whether London loses its position as an international financial centre. If that happens, it will have an influence (on Nomura). But...I believe London will remain an international financial centre," he said.

Asked what chances he saw after the revision in Japan's foreign exchange law due next April, Tsutsui said: "The money flow out of Japan will increase and we'll have more opportunities." --London Newsroom +44 171 542 5107
